item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Wednesday briefing: ​How misinformation and ​a​ hardened immigration policy ​turned Ceuta ​into Europe’s ​latest ​flashpoint
item.description:
In today’s newsletter: The past week shows how quickly images, rumours and ​right-wing political opportunism can eclipse the facts on the ground

Good morning. Last week, an estimated 72,000 migrants began crossing into a tiny Spanish enclave on the tip of Morocco. Within 24 hours, most of them had headed home. At least 88 people died after attempting the crossing, according to local officials. This isn’t the whole story of what happened over the last week, but the facts are worth remembering.

At an emergency meeting yesterday, EU interior ministers sought to draw a line under Ceuta, insisting that the passport-free Schengen area had never been at risk from the arrival of migrants at this scale. Despite this, much of the media coverage has suggested that events in Ceuta represent a territorial threat to Europe, sparking calls for greater security across the region’s borders.

Environment | Eight of the biggest oil companies amassed profits of more than $90bn (£67bn) in just three months as the Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring and the emissions-fuelled climate crisis caused deadly heatwaves.

UK politics | Women should not feel pressurised into experiencing an “ideal birth”, the new health secretary, Yvette Cooper, has said, promising a root-and-branch reform of standards after several damning maternity scandals.

Middle East | Jordan is convening an emergency meeting over an “imminent” threat of an Israeli takeover of the most important Muslim site in Jerusalem, with the potential to “trigger a religious conflict”.

Ukraine | Russian strikes in and around Kyiv killed at least 14 people, ⁠injured 27 and ⁠damaged warehouses, ​emergency service officials said. Some reports put the death toll at 15.

Ceuta | Hundreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] From Michigan to Missouri: Democratic primaries deliver mixed bag on Israel and Gaza
item.description:
From Michigan to Missouri: Democratic primaries deliver mixed bag on Israel and Gaza

Submitted by Victoria Amani Mwaniki Kishoiyian on Wed, 08/05/2026 - 19:06
Besides an upset in Michigan, Democratic candidates endorsed by Aipac defeated progressive challengers
Democratic Congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez addresses reporters on 26 May 2026 in Longview, Washington. She is one of several incumbents who fended off progressive challengers in primaries (Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images/AFP)
Off

The US Democratic Party went to the polls across five states on Tuesday.

The races in Michigan, Missouri, Kansas, Virginia, and Washington were not all solely focused on foreign policy, but the US-Israeli war on Iran and Israel's genocide in Gaza loomed large. The primaries delivered a muddled verdict on how Democratic voters respond to politicians' positions on the issues. 

Michigan produced the evening’s defining result. Former Wayne County health director Abdul El-Sayed defeated Congresswoman Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary for the open Senate seat by roughly one percentage point, 48.5 percent to 47.5 percent. 

Sayed staked out a progressive position on healthcare, but he also put immigration and US foreign policy at the centre of his campaign. He promised to vote to end US military aid to Israel, abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and work to end the Trump administration’s war on Iran, which he argued imperils Americans through the risk of regional war without congressional authorisation. 

Stevens' campaign, by contrast, championed Israel's right to self-defence and supported continued US taxpayer aid. She received firm backing from Democratic establishment figures and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, known as Aipac. Stevens also staked out a hawkish position on Iran. 

Sayed's stance resonated with Wayne County's large Arab American and Muslim electorate. The county includes Dearborn, Hamtramck, and the city of Detroit. Trump made inroads with Wayne County in the 2024 election, including an endorsement from Hamtramck's Yemeni-American mayor.

Former US Vice President Kamala Harris still won the county by a wide margin. 

Missouri: Democratic establishment prevails 

In Missouri, the Democratic establishment defeated a key critic of Israel and the war on Iran.

Former St Louis County prosecutor and incumbent Congressman Wesley Bell defeated former Democratic Congresswoman Cori Bush by 59.2 percent to 36.9 percent in the primary, denying Bush a re-entry to Congress after her defeat for the same seat in 2024. 

Bush was one of Congress’ outspoken advocates for a ceasefire in Gaza. She made the genocide in the enclave and the US war on Iran central pillars of her campaign. 

Bell advocated ironclad support for Israel and was backed by Aipac. 

Kansas: Gazing towards November

The Democrats of Kansas nominated state Senator Cindy Holscher for the seat, while Republicans chose Insurance Commissioner Vicki Schmidt, establishing one of the country’s most potent duels in a state that’s been under the Republican Party's reign for nearly a century. 

Unlike Michigan, foreign policy held little weight in the primary campaign.

Candidates focused on rural development, agriculture, and abortion. 

Virginia: Senator tied to intelligence committee wins

The sole candidate in Virginia’s Democratic primary was former Governor and incumbent Senator Mark Warner, who emphasised his tenure on the Senate Intelligence Committee and attention to national security. Warner is a staunch advocate for Israel and has received support from Aipac. 

Republicans chose former Trump campaign advisor and retired Army Major General Bert Mizusawa in a multi-candidate race.

Warner criticised the absence of congressional consultation surrounding the Trump administration's war on Iran while stating that Iran's nuclear programme presents a significant security threat. 

Virginia has not elected a Republican to the Senate since 2002. 

Washington: Establishment wins again

In Washington, Democratic Congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez fended off a challenge from progressive Brent Hennrich. 

Gluesenkamp Perez was endorsed by Aipac while Hennrich campaigned as a Democrat opposed to the group.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] After Michigan upset, Aipac looks to back Republican candidate against Abdul El-Sayed
item.description:
After Michigan upset, Aipac looks to back Republican candidate against Abdul El-Sayed

Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Wed, 08/05/2026 - 15:39
While this was a race where Israel loomed large, the focus was on how the candidates were funded
US Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks to supporters and the media during a campaign rally in Detroit, Michigan, on 2 August 2026 (Rebecca Cook/Reuters)
Off

After spending more than $30m on a candidate who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary on Wednesday, the leading pro-Israel lobbying group in the US has now indicated it will pivot to the Republican in that race come November. 

The move highlights how the one-issue behemoth does not see itself as ideologically bound to one party or the other. 

"Our members remain determined to ensure that voters reject Dr El-Sayed and his radical anti-Israel agenda," the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) said in a statement. "Our community is proud to support pro-Israel Democrats and Republicans who stand for our values."

The race between pro-Israel Congresswoman Haley Stevens and former Detroit public health official Abdul El-Sayed quickly became the most expensive Democratic primary race of all time.

Stevens was backed by a further $30m from outside groups who bankrolled round-the-clock attack ads on Sayed. 

Sayed, an Egyptian-American Muslim who has never held elected office, won the exceptionally tight race by one percentage point, in what was a stunning upset for establishment Democrats, and a boon to the progressive wave taking hold across the country.

Half a million more Democratic voters showed up to the polls than in previous primary races, which typically see low turnouts, Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said on Wednesday.

Sayed has repeatedly said he's never met with corporate lobbyists. Last quarter, he out-fundraised Stevens in small-dollar donations, according to data analysed by the campaign finance tracker, OpenSecrets. 

"An average of $95 was spent for every vote against Abdul, more than 10 times as much as Abdul’s $9 per vote average," his campaign said in a statement.

But outside spending by groups that don't coordinate with the candidate - which, according to US law, can be unlimited - is how Aipac and other special interest outfits have gained what seemed like a permanent foothold in US politics. 

Craig Holman, government affairs lobbyist for the non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, told Middle East Eye that in 95 percent of US electoral races, "whoever spends the most, wins". 

Thomas Massie's defeat shows Aipac's enduring grip over US Republicans
Read More »

"Yes, money buys elections. It's very effective, and that's why these candidates work overtime continually raising money," he said. 

Few groups are willing to spend as much as Aipac does - especially in a climate where emboldened criticism of Israel has proliferated both the left and the right of the political spectrum in the US. 

In 2022, Aipac helped Stevens secure her seat in the House of Representatives by ousting longtime lawmaker Andy Levin for his support of US policies to punish violent Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

"Today, Michigan launched a new chapter in our political history," Levin wrote on his Instagram account on Wednesday, accompanied by a photograph of him hugging Sayed.

"Out with all the big money, dark money and corporate and special interest control of our politics. We the people hunger for authenticity."

Earlier this year, Aipac helped oust Republican Thomas Massie, who voted against US foreign aid to Israel, in his Kentucky primary race by spending more than $4m against him through its United Democracy Project political action committee.

That was just part of a coalition of pro-Israel groups that spent $9m against him. 

'Truth and justice'

The IMEU Policy Project - an outfit less than three years old that advocates for Palestinian rights - revealed that it contributed $400,000 in support of Sayed's campaign.

Sayed has described Israel's nearly three-year-old assault on Gaza as a genocide, echoing language used by leading human rights organisations, genocide scholars and the United Nations.

Israel, as well as most US lawmakers, reject the term. 

His position resonated strongly with many voters in Michigan who played a crucial role in organising against former President Joe Biden during the 2024 election, given his immovable support for Israel, even as Palestinian casualties mounted in the tens of thousands.

Certain suburbs of Detroit, which house more than 200,000 registered Arab-American voters, voted overwhelmingly for Donald Trump at the time.

This was despite Wayne County on the whole backing Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris with more than 62 percent of the vote. But Trump ended up winning the entire state by just over one percentage point. 

"People in Michigan, they're looking for leaders that are going to call out bold solutions and that are going to try and speak out against the status quo because the status quo hasn't been working," Alabas Farhat, a member of the Michigan House of Representatives who appeared in a social media video backing Sayed, told MEE. 

"The status quo has led to our state being 49th in unemployment. It's led to us being 47th in third grade literacy. It's led to our middle class having less wealth than they did in previous years," he added.

"Trump came along, and he sold a false bag of goods, but he was at least willing to say things were wrong. Now comes Abdul El-Sayed, somebody who has made truth and justice two central pillars to his campaign." 

The tactic is similar to that of a recent spate of winning progressive Democratic candidates around the country, from New York to New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Colorado. 

But according to Sally Howell, an expert on Arab American Studies at the University of Michigan-Dearborn, Sayed's polling numbers actually went up after he pivoted away from incessant talk of Aipac funding and moved to getting "money out of politics" entirely - a tagline that became central to his campaign. 

"He started talking about not getting money from DTE, the energy company here in Michigan... and this issue of the AI data centres, and how they would drive up our water bills," she said.

"These are issues that really matter" to Michiganders across the political spectrum, she added.  

America considers electing its first Muslim governor: Abdulrahman El-Sayed
Read More »

In his victory speech on Wednesday, Sayed said he spoke to Stevens and was assured of her endorsement as he gears up to face former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers in November. 

Hertel, the state Democratic Party chair, insisted in his remarks that Democrats are now "united" to defeat Donald Trump-backed candidates in November.

The outcome of that vote may tip the balance of the US Senate, and turn the chamber blue for the final two years of President Trump's term in office. 

If Sayed wins, he would become the very first Muslim elected to the upper chamber on Capitol Hill.

Writing on his social media platform Truth Social on Wednesday, Trump called Sayed "a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel", but added that his win is also "great news for the Republican party", suggesting that he will be easy to defeat.

"I think that it's going to go a lot darker than the negative campaigning we've seen, and it's going to be very anti-Arab and a lot more Islamophobic," Howell said of the race between now and November. 

For his part, Sayed told supporters and the media on Wednesday that the focus on his name and identity is "the only play they got" against him. 

"It's like, wow, he's different," he said of Republican attacks.

"That's the best you got? You can't actually talk about what you want to do? My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can't afford your groceries."

item.description:
Trump clashed with Hegseth over munition shortage amid war on Iran: Report

US President Donald Trump confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Washington's critical shortage during the war on Iran, The Washington Post reported.

According to the newspaper citing sources, Trump demanded answers during a cabinet meeting last week after finding out about the deficit in vital weapons, despite his understanding that the issue had been addressed. 

The report cited the shortage in munitions as one of the reasons behind Trump's decision to pause large-scale strikes against Iran.

During the meeting, Hegseth reportedly defended himself and instead blamed Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg for the shortages and "for not ensuring Trump was fully apprised" about the state of Washinton's stockpiles.

The White House denied the report, with press secretary Karoline Leavitt calling it "100% fake news", adding that Trump saying "has the utmost confidence" in Hegseth.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Nearly 80% of US army's interceptors for a key missile defense system depleted: Report
item.description:
Nearly 80% of US army's interceptors for a key missile defense system depleted: Report

The US army has used up nearly 80 percent of its interceptors for a key missile defence system, CNN reported citing several sources familiar with the matter. 

According to the report, senior US military officials warned that the Pentagon’s munitions stockpile is "dangerously low," with key air defence systems particularly depleted during the war on Iran.

The US military exhausted nearly four-fifths of its THAAD missile inventory compared to pre-war figures. Meanwhile, half of its Patriot interceptors were burned through since the start of the war. 

One source familiar with recent internal Pentagon reports noted that the army used "virtually all" of its highly accurate long-range, surface-to-air weapons in the same period.

item.description:
Trump slams reports on munition shortages, says US army has 'massive amounts' of weapons

Donald Trump has hit back on media reports of depleting munitions, insisting that the army has large stockpiles and expaning manufacturing. 

"The U.S. has massive amounts of 'munitions,' especially of certain types," he said in a post on his social media platform Truth Social, adding that "large amounts" are being manufactured and shipped over to the country "as needed".

"Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history," Trump said. 

He also threatened that "'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down," and wrote that "long term jail sentences will be sought".
